## Design

### 2026-10-09 – After evaluating the initial design, I chose to move beyond a basic RP2040-based analyzer and upgrade to the RP2350A, providing additional SRAM and more programmable I/O resources for the capture syst

**2h**

After evaluating the initial design, I chose to move beyond a basic RP2040-based analyzer and upgrade to the RP2350A, providing additional SRAM and more programmable I/O resources for the capture system. The current design targets eight digital input channels compatible with 3.3 V and 5 V logic signals, with the goal of capturing digital activity and transferring recorded traces to a computer over USB.

To make the instrument more usable, I expanded the design to include a TFT display and three rotary encoders. These will eventually provide a local interface for monitoring capture status, navigating settings, selecting channels, and configuring capture parameters. The computer will remain the primary interface for detailed waveform analysis.

I began developing the schematic in KiCad and added the main components: the RP2350A microcontroller, USB-C receptacle, SN74LVC245A eight-channel buffer, USBLC6-2SC6 USB ESD protection device, external W25Q16 flash memory, and a 12 MHz crystal. I also started selecting the associated passive components and connectors from Robu.in while keeping the overall project within the $65 Tier 2 budget.

Input protection became an important part of the design. I selected the SN74LVC245A as a candidate for buffering the eight input channels and investigated suitable ESD protection. After comparing available components, I shortlisted two TPD4E1U06 devices to protect all eight exposed inputs. For USB protection, I checked the USBLC6-2SC6 datasheet and began planning its placement and connections near the USB-C connector.
Oh oh and  I also learned to distinguish between passive crystals and active clock oscillators, identifying a 12 MHz, 10 ppm SMD crystal as a more promising candidate, over accidentally choosing a 27.12 MHz crystal randomly 😭.
